summary: Told that his mother and brothers are outside, Jesus names as his family those who hear the word of God and do it.

context.title: Mother and brothers
paragraphs: Matthew and Mark tell a similar scene before the parables; Luke places it after them. [c1] Farrar doubts it is the same incident, though he allows that Luke may have moved it; Meyer reads Luke as following Mark in a shortened form. [c20][c2] Luke leaves out the motive Mark gives, that the family set out to take hold of Jesus because it was said he was beside himself. [c3]

In Luke the visit closes the teaching on the sower. [c4] The seed is the word of God, the good soil are those who hear the word and hold it fast, and the next saying warns hearers to take care how they hear. [c5] The family’s arrival gives Jesus the occasion to name who the good soil are. [c4]

The saying does not set Mary aside. [c6] Luke has already shown her accepting the angel’s word and keeping these things in her heart, and Bengel, on the parallel saying in 11:28, remarks that she herself kept the word. [c6] The Pulpit Commentary draws the lesson that there is something “more solemn even than family ties”, holy as they are. [c7]

translationNotes.summary: Adelphoi means brothers, but biblical usage stretches the word to near kin; how these were related is disputed.
translationNotes.body: Adelphos means brother, but like Hebrew ach it can cover any kinsman, as when Lot is called Abraham’s brother. [c8] Three old readings exist: cousins, the Latin view since Jerome; sons of Joseph by a first marriage, held by many Greek Fathers; and sons of Joseph and Mary, the view of Helvidius. [c9] Catholic tradition, which holds Mary’s perpetual virginity, rejects the last; Thayer argues for it. [c10] The word alone does not settle the question. [c11]

translationNotes.summary: In the SBL Greek text the verb is singular, though its subject is “his mother and his brethren”.
translationNotes.body: In the SBL Greek text the verb is singular, though its subject is the mother and the brothers together. [c12] The Greek text used by the Cambridge Bible has the plural instead. [c12] The Cambridge Bible observes that the singular reading would give Mary a specially prominent part in the visit. [c13]

translationNotes.summary: Where Mark and Matthew speak of God’s will, Luke speaks of the word of God, the seed of the sower parable.
translationNotes.body: Mark ends the scene with doing the will of God, and Matthew with the will of the Father, but Luke has hearing the word of God. [c14] The phrase reaches back to 8:11, where the seed is the word of God. [c15] Ellicott takes it in its widest sense, every form in which a revelation from God reaches the human mind. [c16]

translationNotes.summary: Hearing has to issue in doing: Luke pairs the two verbs here and in 6:47.
translationNotes.body: Luke pairs hearing with doing here, as he does in 6:47 at the close of the Sermon on the Plain. [c17] In 11:28 Jesus likewise calls blessed those who hear the word of God and keep it. [c18] The Cambridge Bible puts the point sharply: “hearing without obedience was more than valueless”. [c19] The Pulpit Commentary adds that this greater blessedness is open to all who will. [c18]

claims.text: Matthew 12:46-50 and Mark 3:31-35 report a similar scene to Luke 8:19-21, but Luke places it after the teaching in parables and the other two Gospels before.
Luke gives the section in accordance with Mark, but in a shortened form.
Mark 3:21 gives the fullest account of the family’s motive, that they went out to seize him because it was said he was beside himself; Luke’s shortened account does not include it.
In Luke the connection is topical: the visit gives Jesus occasion to indicate who represent the good, fruitful soil of the parable of the sower.
In Luke 8:11 the seed is the word of God, in 8:15 the good soil are those who hear the word and hold it fast, and 8:18 warns hearers to take heed how they hear.

Luke presents Mary as accepting the angel’s word (1:38) and keeping these things in her heart (2:19); Bengel, commenting on the parallel saying in Luke 11:28, remarks that she herself kept the word and was blessed for it, so the saying does not set her aside.
The Pulpit Commentary draws from Luke 8:21 the lesson that there is something more solemn even than family ties, holy and binding though they are.
Ἀδελφός means a brother but, like the Hebrew אָח, can denote any blood relation or kinsman, as in Genesis 14:16, where Lot is called Abraham’s brother.

Three views of the brethren of the Lord are old: the Latins (with few exceptions) hold they were cousins, the majority of the Greek Fathers took them as sons of Joseph by a first marriage, and Helvidius held they were sons of Joseph and Mary.
Catholic tradition, which holds Mary’s perpetual virginity, holds that the brethren were not sons of Joseph and Mary, while Thayer’s lexicon argues that they were own brothers born after Jesus.
The word brethren by itself furnishes no certain indication of the exact relationship.
The SBL Greek New Testament reads the singular Παρεγένετο in Luke 8:19, while the Greek text used by the Cambridge Bible reads a plural.
The Cambridge Bible notes that the singular reading would imply that Mary took a specially prominent part in the incident.
Where Mark 3:35 has doing the will of God and Matthew 12:50 the will of my Father, Luke 8:21 has hearing and doing the word of God.
The phrase λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ in Luke 8:21 recalls Luke 8:11, where the seed is the word of God.
Ellicott takes the word of God in Luke 8 in its widest sense, including every form by which a revelation from God is conveyed to the mind.
Luke 6:47, at the close of the Sermon on the Plain, also pairs hearing and doing Jesus’ words.
Luke 11:28 calls blessed those who hear the word of God and keep it, a saying parallel to Luke 8:21; the Pulpit Commentary notes that all may attain this blessedness.
The Cambridge Bible comments that hearing without obedience was more than valueless.
Farrar in the Cambridge Bible says the incident can hardly be the same as Mark 3:31-35 and Matthew 12:46-50, though he allows that Luke may have misplaced it.
